strengths: The core technical contribution is clean and well-executed: Theorem 4.4 shows the PLD of the random-allocation mixture is the log of a sum of exponentiated PLDs of the dominating pair, reducing the problem to convolutions of exp-PLDs, and Lemma 4.5 shows this convolution preserves (α,β)-tightness of stochastic domination — unlike ordinary PLD convolution where errors accumulate.

The paper delivers on a concrete, important gap: prior analyses of k-out-of-t random allocation (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025; Dong et al. 2025) yield only loose RDP/hockey-stick bounds with lossy conversions, and prior empirical evidence (Chua et al. 2024a; Choquette-Choo et al. 2025) relied on Monte Carlo that provides no formal guarantees. This work gives the first efficient, formally valid, and demonstrably tight numerical accounting for this scheme.

The PLD realization abstraction (Defn. 3.1, Theorem 3.3) is a genuine conceptual contribution: it extends domination-preserving numerical accounting from composition to Poisson subsampling directly on PLDs, removing the dependence on analytic subsampled-Gaussian/Laplace expressions in existing accounting libraries and enabling arbitrary noise distributions.

Evaluation is thorough and convincing: upper bounds nearly coincide with matched numerical lower bounds (Remark 4.7), agree with Monte Carlo in statistically stable regimes, beat all prior analytic bounds, and runtime matches the O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²) theory (Fig. 3). The PREAMBLE case study (Fig. 5) demonstrates practical value on a real composite algorithm where RDP-based accounting is substantially loose.
Reproducibility is strong: full algorithmic details (Alg. 1–9), all proofs in appendices, complete experimental settings in Appendix D, and a released implementation (Shenfeld, 2026).

Limitations are handled honestly and constructively: the FFT-vs-multiplicative-grid tradeoff (Section 5, Fig. 8), float-precision stability limits for very small δ, lossiness of the k-to-⌊t/k⌋ reduction (Fig. 11), and the fact that Poisson and allocation privacy profiles are incomparable in some regimes (Fig. 7) are all explicitly discussed rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The conceptual framework (dominating randomizer, reduction of k-out-of-t to k=1, dominating pair for random allocation) is imported from Feldman & Shenfeld (2025); the paper's novelty is the numerical/algorithmic layer and the PLD realization notion rather than new privacy theory, which somewhat limits its reach.

The headline claim that random allocation is 'at least as good as Poisson subsampling' in privacy-utility tradeoff is conditional: the privacy profiles are formally incomparable in some regimes (Fig. 7), and the tradeoff claim must combine the paper's privacy bounds with utility results from prior work (Chua et al. 2024a); the abstract states it more strongly than the nuance in the body warrants.

The direct O(n²) convolution per step, while robust to the large dynamic range of exp-PLDs, is asymptotically and practically more expensive than FFT-based methods in some regimes (acknowledged), and the PREAMBLE evaluation required 10^6 bins and heavy computation — suggesting scalability limits for very large compositions.

For k > 1, results inherit the lossy reduction of Lemma 2.8 and are shown to be slightly suboptimal when the rounding error t mod (t/k) is non-negligible (Fig. 11); no tighter treatment of general k is provided.

Tightness is established empirically via matched lower bounds rather than a formal optimality result for the discretization scheme; this is standard practice for numerical accounting but leaves a formal gap.
Evaluation is heavily focused on the Gaussian mechanism (motivated by the applications); while the framework is general, other noise distributions are only argued for, not extensively evaluated.

strengths: The paper develops a genuinely new technical tool—the notion of a PLD realization—that allows numerical privacy accounting operations beyond composition (subsampling and random allocation) to be performed directly on discretized privacy loss distributions while provably preserving domination. This is a clean and useful conceptual contribution that fills a real gap in the PLD toolkit.

The core result (Theorem 4.4) giving an exact identity between the PLD of the 1-out-of-t random allocation and a log-sum of exponentiated PLDs is elegant, and the accompanying algorithm comes with a full runtime and tightness analysis (Theorem 4.6: O((IQR/α)²·log³t)), which is rare for numerical accounting methods—most prior work lacks formal accuracy guarantees.

The evaluation is thorough and compares against essentially all relevant baselines: prior analytic bounds (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025; Dong et al. 2025), Monte Carlo estimates, lower bounds from Chua et al. 2024a, and Poisson sampling. Upper and lower bounds nearly coincide, giving strong evidence of tightness, and the appendix covers k>1, FFT variants, runtime/accuracy trade-offs, and stability considerations.

The paper is honest about trade-offs that many works would hide, e.g., that FFT convolution is superior in some regimes, that stochastic domination is not preserved under the dual/subsampling transformations (Claim B.2), and numerical stability issues near machine precision. Code is referenced, aiding reproducibility.
The application to the nested sampling in PREAMBLE (Asi et al. 2025) demonstrates real practical value: the PLD accounting substantially improves on RDP-based bounds even under heavy composition.
weaknesses: The contribution is incremental relative to very recent concurrent work. The overall framework (dominating pair reduction, k-to-1 reduction in Lemma 2.8, the dominating pair in Claim 2.9) is taken essentially wholesale from Feldman & Shenfeld (2025), and the novelty is confined to the numerical computation layer. The paper is best viewed as an engineering/numerical extension of that line rather than a new conceptual advance, which limits its significance for a broad ML audience.

The practical evaluation is narrow: all headline experiments use the Gaussian mechanism. Although the method is stated for arbitrary PLD realizations, there is little evidence of its behavior for other noise distributions or non-Gaussian dominating pairs, where the dynamic-range properties of the multiplicative discretization (the stated motivation for avoiding FFT) may differ substantially.

The direct convolution approach costs O(n²) per step, and the paper itself reports needing 10⁶ bins for the PREAMBLE experiment with 'heavy computation load'. The claimed efficiency over RDP-based accounting comes at considerable practical cost, and the FFT comparison (which would be O(n log n)) is relegated to the appendix without tightness guarantees for the FFT variant.

The reduction for k > 1 (Lemma 2.8) is lossy, particularly when t/k is small, and the paper only empirically observes the resulting suboptimality (Figure 11) rather than characterizing or mitigating it.

There is no dedicated limitations section; caveats (lossy k>1 reduction, floating-point stability below δ ≈ 10⁻¹⁵, FFT tightness gaps) are scattered through Sections 5 and the appendix. Some notation is dense (e.g., the add/remove direction markers) and hurts readability of an already specialized paper.

The significance of the improvement over Poisson sampling is modest—the privacy profiles are close and the paper itself notes they are incomparable in general—so the headline claim that random allocation is 'better suited for DP-SGD' rests largely on utility results from prior work rather than contributions of this paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important problem: tight numerical privacy accounting for random allocation (balls-and-bins / k-out-of-t) subsampling in DP-SGD, which prior work (Feldman & Shenfeld 2025; Dong et al. 2025) could only handle via lossy (ε,δ) or Rényi-DP bounds with 10-20% overheads.

The core technical insight is elegant: the PLD of the mixture arising in random allocation equals a logarithm of a sum of exponentiated PLDs of the dominating pair (Theorem 4.4), which reduces the computation to t-wise convolutions of exp-PLDs. This yields a clean algorithm with provable (α,β)-tightness and runtime O(log³(t)·log(t/β)/α²) (Theorem 4.6).

The PLD realization framework (Section 3, Theorem 3.3) is a genuinely useful conceptual contribution: it makes domination-preserving Poisson subsampling a first-class operation on discretized PLDs, extending PLD-based accounting beyond composition and enabling accounting for arbitrary noise distributions rather than only analytically-derived subsampled Gaussian/Laplace mechanisms.

The evaluation is convincing and carefully validates tightness: the paper constructs numerical lower bounds (Remark 4.7) that nearly coincide with the upper bounds, matches Monte Carlo estimates in regimes where those are statistically stable, and demonstrates concrete downstream impact by improving accounting for the PREAMBLE DP-SGD scheme (Figure 5), including a real setting (ε=1, δ=10⁻⁶, many composition rounds) where tightness of the base PLD matters.

The results support a meaningful conclusion for practice: random allocation is never worse than Poisson subsampling in the explored regimes (Figure 1), matching the MC evidence of Chua et al. (2024a) and Choquette-Choo et al. (2025) but now with formal guarantees.

Implementation details are fully specified (Appendix C, Algorithms 1-9), including numerical stability mitigations (Kahan summation, logsf/logcdf), and an implementation is released; runtime experiments on a laptop confirm the theoretical complexity analysis (Figure 3), supporting reproducibility.

The manuscript is honest about limitations of the approach, e.g., that stochastic domination is not preserved under dual/subsampling transformations (Claim B.2), that FFT-based convolution lacks tightness guarantees, and that the k-out-of-t reduction via Lemma 2.8 introduces rounding suboptimality (Figure 11).
weaknesses: The work is heavily built on the concurrent reductions of Feldman & Shenfeld (2025) and Dong et al. (2025): the dominating-pair reduction (Claims 2.7, 2.9), the reduction from general k to k=1 (Lemma 2.8), and the overall problem framing all come from prior work. The genuinely new technical content is Theorem 4.4, Lemma 4.5, and the discretization/convolution algorithm — a solid but somewhat incremental advance over the prior landscape.

The evaluation is almost entirely restricted to the Gaussian mechanism (the authors acknowledge this), so the claimed generality ('PLD of random allocation applied to any differentially private algorithm') is only demonstrated for the one case with a convenient log-normal exp-PLD structure; behavior for heavier-tailed or discrete mechanisms is not explored.

The direct convolution approach is O(n²) per step, which, while acceptable in practice (seconds on a laptop), is asymptotically worse than FFT-based composition methods; the FFT alternative is discussed but lacks tightness guarantees, so the method's efficiency story has a caveat in regimes demanding very small α or very large t (e.g., the PREAMBLE experiment required 10⁶ bins and heavy computation).

Tightness guarantees rely on stochastic domination, which the authors show is not preserved under the dual and subsampling transformations (Claim B.2); only the approximate form is preserved, so a small amount of slack (β) accumulates through compositions, which is handled but adds analytical complexity and means the framework is not fully lossless end-to-end.

Some presentation issues: minor typos and grammatical slips ('thar', 'the reminder t mod k', 'a PLD realizations', missing URL for the Shenfeld 2026 code reference), and the notion of (α,β)-tight domination, while well-motivated, requires careful tracking of error accumulation across discretization steps that makes the tightness argument (Theorem 4.6) somewhat intricate to verify.

The claim that random allocation is 'at least as good as' Poisson subsampling is parameter-regime dependent (the schemes are incomparable, as the authors themselves show in Figure 7 for ε ≪ 1 and ε → ∞); the abstract/introduction could be more precise about the scope of this conclusion.
